claim: `tar` bundles files, with their permissions and timestamps, into one archive.
reasoning: GNU tar stores each member's mode and mtime in the archive header. Verified empirically on this machine: a file created mode 640 and archived with `gtar -czf` lists back as `-rw-r----- yutaasakura/wheel 6 2026-08-11 06:42 etc/conf` under `gtar -tvzf`, i.e. permissions and timestamp are preserved in the archive.

claim: `tar` `-c` means create.
reasoning: `gtar --help` on this machine prints `-c, --create  create a new archive`.

claim: `tar` `-x` means extract.
reasoning: `gtar --help` prints `-x, --extract, --get  extract files from an archive`.

claim: `tar` `-f` names the archive file.
reasoning: `gtar --help` prints `-f, --file=ARCHIVE  use archive file or device ARCHIVE`.

claim: `tar` `-z` filters the archive through gzip.
reasoning: `gtar --help` prints `-z, --gzip, --gunzip, --ungzip  filter the archive through gzip`. Empirically, `gtar -czf` produced output identified by file(1) as `gzip compressed data`.

claim: `-g` / `--listed-incremental=FILE` keeps a snapshot file so later `tar` runs archive only what changed since the previous dump — stated in the Commands table as an option of `tar` with no implementation qualifier.
reasoning: The semantics are right for GNU tar (`gtar --help`: `-g, --listed-incremental=FILE  handle new GNU-format incremental backup`; empirically, a second dump against the same snapshot file contained only `etc/` and the newly added `etc/new`). The universality was wrong: this is a GNU extension. On this machine's system tar (bsdtar 3.5.3, the default on macOS) `tar -g ...` exits 1 with a usage message and `--listed-incremental=` fails with `tar: Option --listed-incremental=... is not supported`. The neighbouring Traps paragraph already qualifies the compression flags as GNU behaviour but the table did not qualify `-g`. Fixed: the cell now reads `-g` / `--listed-incremental=FILE` (GNU tar only).
source: GNU tar 1.35 --help and bsdtar 3.5.3 empirical runs; https://www.gnu.org/software/tar/manual/tar.html#Incremental-Dumps

claim: Worked example `tar -czf /backup/etc.tar.gz /etc` produces a gzip-compressed archive of the named directory.
reasoning: Clustered `-czf ARCHIVE PATH` is valid: `-f` consumes the next argument. Reproduced with the same shape against a scratch tree (`gtar -czf /tmp/etc-test.tar.gz etc`), producing a gzip file whose listing contains the directory and its members with modes and timestamps intact.

claim: GNU `tar` compresses only when told to: `-z`, `-j` and `-J` select gzip, bzip2 and xz respectively, so a plain `-cf` archive is bundled but not compressed.
reasoning: `gtar --help` prints `-j, --bzip2  filter the archive through bzip2`, `-J, --xz  filter the archive through xz`, `-z, --gzip ... filter the archive through gzip`. Empirically `gtar -cf /tmp/plain.tar etc` produced a file identified by file(1) as `POSIX tar archive (GNU)`, not a compressed stream.

claim: `rsync` copies or synchronises a directory tree to another path or host, sending only the differences.
reasoning: The official rsync man page's opening description: rsync "is famous for its delta-transfer algorithm, which reduces the amount of data sent over the network by sending only the differences between the source files and the existing files in the destination," and it accepts local and remote (host:path) destinations.

claim: `rsync -a` is archive mode, equivalent to `-rlptgoD`.
reasoning: rsync(1): "--archive, -a  archive mode is -rlptgoD (no -A,-X,-U,-N,-H)" and, in the option body, "This is equivalent to -rlptgoD." (The man page notes one exception: with --files-from, -r is not implied — not a case the guide asserts anything about.)

claim: `--delete` removes files from the destination that no longer exist on the source, so a deletion on the source is applied to the copy.
reasoning: rsync(1) --delete: "This tells rsync to delete extraneous files from the receiving side (ones that aren't on the sending side), but only for the directories that are being synchronized." That is exactly the propagation behaviour the guide warns about.

claim: `-n` / `--dry-run` is a trial run with no changes.
reasoning: rsync(1) summary line: "--dry-run, -n  perform a trial run with no changes made"; body: "This makes rsync perform a trial run that doesn't make any changes." Short and long forms are paired exactly as the guide pairs them.

claim: `--link-dest=DIR` hardlinks unchanged files against a previous copy.
reasoning: rsync(1): "--link-dest=DIR  hardlink to files in DIR when unchanged"; body: "unchanged files are hard linked from DIR to the destination directory." The `=DIR` form the guide shows is the man page's own spelling.

claim: Worked example `rsync -a --delete /srv/data/ backup:/srv/data/` mirrors a local tree to the same path on a remote host.
reasoning: The host:path destination form and the trailing-slash source form are both standard rsync usage documented in the man page's USAGE section (e.g. `rsync -av /src/foo/ /dest/foo`, `rsync -avz foo:src/bar/ /data/tmp`). With `-a --delete` the destination becomes a mirror of the source directory's contents, which is the reading the surrounding prose gives it.

claim: `rsync -a` does not preserve ACLs (`-A`), extended attributes (`-X`), or hardlinks (`-H`).
reasoning: rsync(1) --archive body, verbatim: "Be aware that it does not include preserving ACLs (-A), xattrs (-X), atimes (-U), crtimes (-N), nor the finding and preserving of hardlinks (-H)." The three short flags are paired with the right meanings (`--acls, -A`; `--xattrs, -X`; `--hard-links, -H`).

claim: A trailing slash on an `rsync` source copies that directory's contents into the destination; omitting it creates the directory itself inside the destination.
reasoning: rsync(1): "A trailing slash on the source changes this behavior to avoid creating an additional directory level at the destination. You can think of a trailing / on a source as meaning 'copy the contents of this directory' as opposed to 'copy the directory by name'." The man page's own equivalence `rsync -av /src/foo /dest` == `rsync -av /src/foo/ /dest/foo` confirms the no-slash case creates /dest/foo.

claim: A mistaken `rm` is a deletion a snapshot can roll back (the only other command invocation in the file).
reasoning: `rm` removes directory entries / files, per POSIX rm and GNU coreutils rm; the guide makes no claim about any rm option. Recorded for completeness because it is the only remaining inline command span in the file.
